about.notes: The abstract describes the full set of 448 questions and does not name a Diamond subset.
about.what_it_tests: GPQA is a set of 448 multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry, written by domain experts. The questions are written so that experts in the matching field can answer many of them, while skilled non-experts still miss most of them even with unrestricted access to the web. Model results are reported as accuracy. The abstract describes this full set and does not name a smaller subset.

about.maintainer: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, Julian Michael and Samuel R. Bowman
about.notes: Maintainer detail: GPQA authors. The arXiv abstract page does not mention a Diamond subset, so its definition was not confirmed here. The 448-question count and the expert and non-expert accuracies come from the page. Publisher-printed results from several labs are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: GPQA is a set of 448 multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by experts with or working toward PhDs in those fields. Domain experts reached about 65% accuracy, while skilled non-experts with web access reached about 34%, which is why the questions are described as hard to answer by search alone. The Diamond subset is a smaller, harder selection of these questions.

about.notes: The dataset card is OpenAI's own page: it names OpenAI as creator and lists 4/12/2025 as the initial publish date, so introduced is 2025. The Epoch AI review's 2026 dates refer to its own review and to later bug-fix entries on the card (2/27/26). The card points to the GPT-4.1 blog post for results; that post was not opened. The 128k and 256k-1M ranges come from the catalog labels and the card's file split. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: GraphWalks gives a model a directed graph as a long edge list and asks one graph question in a single answer, with no tools. The two task types are a breadth-first search from a start node to a given depth, which returns only the nodes at exactly that depth, and a parents query, which returns the nodes with an edge pointing into a given node. The public dataset has 1,150 examples, split into inputs of 128k and shorter and inputs from 256k to 1M. Each answer ends with a 'Final Answer:' line of node IDs and is scored by recall, precision and F1 against the true set.

about.maintainer: Gray Swan with the UK AI Security Institute, the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and model developers
about.notes: Cited in Claude Sonnet 5.5 System Card section 5.2.1 as arXiv:2603.15714. Paper not read.
about.what_it_tests: Probability that an attacker finds a successful indirect prompt injection after k attempts, across coding, tool use and GUI computer use.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (27 October 2021) describes the problems and the verifier training.
about.what_it_tests: GSM8K tests multi-step arithmetic reasoning with about 8,500 grade-school math word problems. The score is the share of problems with the correct final answer, usually with a stated number of few-shot examples.

about.notes: The xAI Grok 4.7 model card could not be retrieved: the data.x.ai URL that was guessed returned 404 and no search result gave the card's address. The launch page is the only primary source found. An aggregator (BenchLM) describes a HackerBench v0.2 measuring benign refusal, which the launch page does not mention; that version is not confirmed and is not described here. The year of introduction is not stated.
about.what_it_tests: The xAI Grok 4.7 launch page calls HackerBench v0.3 its own benchmark for risky and malicious cyber tasks. The reported result is the share of risky dual-use prompts that the model let through, and the page says Grok 4.7 let through 3.3 percent while showing the highest safety of the models compared. The page does not explain how prompts are built or how each answer is judged.

about.maintainer: Tianrui Guan, Fuxiao Liu, and co-authors (University of Maryland, College Park)
about.notes: Question-pair accuracy is stricter than the per-question accuracy, so a single printed number can be either one.
about.what_it_tests: HallusionBench tests whether a model reasons from the image or falls back on language priors and visual illusions. Human experts wrote 1,129 yes/no questions on 346 figures, mixing original images, edited images, charts, tables, maps, and illusions, and arranged them as control pairs. Each answer is marked correct or not. The paper then reports accuracy over all questions, accuracy over a whole figure, and question-pair accuracy, which counts a pair only when the model is right on every image in that pair.

about.notes: The arXiv page (submitted 28 July 2026, revised 3 August 2026) gives the task count, the handbook lengths, the tools and the strict grading; it does not print an affiliation, and the released code sits under the surge-ai GitHub organisation. Moonshot AI ran it with the official OpenHands-based harness on the early open-source v1 tasks.
about.what_it_tests: HANDBOOK.md tests whether an agent follows a long company policy document while doing multi-step tool work. Each of the 65 tasks sits in a self-contained company environment with a handbook of 20 to 124 pages and mock email, chat, calendar, issue-tracking and commerce services reached over the Model Context Protocol. A trial passes only when every programmatic criterion is met (824 criteria in total).

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (open-source repository harveyai/harvey-labs); Artificial Analysis and Mercor run separate third-party evaluations. Announced May 6, 2026, and launched without a leaderboard. Task counts differ across sources: the page cites 1,200 and 1,250 tasks, Mercor lists 1,749. Third-party rankings exist (Mercor, and an Artificial Analysis private set of 120 tasks). The 'Google, xAI printed' labels were not confirmed in a model card.
about.what_it_tests: Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark tests AI agents on long, multi-step legal work. Each task gives the agent a short instruction and a client matter with case files, and asks for a work product that a reviewing lawyer would check, across more than 1,200 tasks in 24 legal practice areas. Expert-written rubrics grade each deliverable, and a task counts as passed only when every criterion passes.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: developed with 262 physicians from 60 countries. Paper: arXiv 2505.08775 (May 2025). Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. The paper uses GPT-4.1 as the automatic rubric scorer. The GPT-6 Astra system card reports HealthBench as a length-adjusted score, where higher is better.
about.what_it_tests: HealthBench tests how well an AI model answers health conversations, such as those with patients or clinicians, judged against detailed rubrics written by physicians. It has 5,000 multi-turn conversations and 48,562 rubric criteria, each with a weight that reflects how much a physician would value it. An automatic grader scores each reply against the rubric, and the benchmark includes subsets named Consensus and Hard.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: rubrics written and adjudicated by three or more physicians across three phases. Paper: arXiv 2604.27470. OpenAI built the benchmark and also reports results for its own clinician product, so it is not an independent test; the caveat appears in secondary coverage. xAI's Grok 4.7 launch page does report HealthBench Professional (56.7 percent for Grok 4.7). The 'length-adjusted' label is confirmed for HealthBench, not for HealthBench Professional, where the GPT-6 Astra card says only 'higher is better'. Aggregator leaderboards disagree on the top model, so no score is given.
about.what_it_tests: HealthBench Professional tests AI models on real conversations that clinicians had with an AI assistant, in three areas: care consultation, writing and documentation, and medical research. Each example is scored against rubrics written and checked by at least three physicians. It is meant to be hard, and about a third of the examples were chosen because physicians deliberately tried to find failures.

about.maintainer: University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI (Rowan Zellers and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (19 May 2019) describes the adversarial construction.
about.what_it_tests: HellaSwag tests commonsense inference: the model reads the start of an everyday situation and picks the most plausible continuation from several candidates, where the wrong ones were machine-written to fool models. The score is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament (student organizers at Harvard and MIT)
about.notes: The competition dates from 1998; its use as a model benchmark is a convention of model publishers rather than a release by the organizers, and the introduced year is left empty for that reason. Different publishers may use different attempt counts (single answer, or an average over several samples) and should not be compared without reading the setup.
about.what_it_tests: HMMT is a long-running high-school mathematics competition held twice a year, in November and February, with the February tournament the harder of the two. As a benchmark, the problems of one tournament (release pages name the February 2025 contest) are given to a model, and the score is the share of problems answered correctly, usually without tools.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (7 July 2021) introduced it together with Codex.
about.what_it_tests: HumanEval tests Python code generation with 164 hand-written programming problems given as function signatures and docstrings, each checked by unit tests. The score is the share of problems solved, usually pass@1.

about.maintainer: Center for AI Safety (CAIS) and Scale AI
about.notes: The arXiv preprint is 2501.14249 (January 2025); a later version was published in Nature in February 2026 under the title 'A benchmark of expert-level academic questions to assess AI capabilities'. Question counts differ by source (2,500 in the paper; about 3,000 in press coverage), so the paper's figure is used. The family label 'HLE with tools' is a configuration of the same benchmark and is not described separately.
about.what_it_tests: Humanity's Last Exam is a test of about 2,500 expert-level questions across dozens of subjects, including mathematics, the humanities and the natural sciences. The items are multiple-choice or short-answer, so answers can be graded automatically. It was built because leading models had passed more than 90 percent of older tests, and at launch the most capable models scored below 10 percent.

about.notes: A Hypersim cell on a model card is not, by itself, the semantic-segmentation or 3D-shape score from this paper.
about.what_it_tests: Hypersim is a photorealistic synthetic dataset for indoor scene understanding, not a question-answering test. It has 77,400 images of 461 indoor scenes, with per-pixel depth, surface normals, instance labels, camera information, and a split of each image into reflectance, illumination, and a residual lighting term. The paper uses the images as pre-training and then scores transfer to semantic segmentation and to 3D shape prediction. It does not define the single unnamed number some model cards print in a Hypersim cell.

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington
about.notes: Maintainer detail: Valentina Pyatkin and co-authors. Title of the paper: 'Generalizing Verifiable Instruction Following', published at NeurIPS 2025 (Datasets and Benchmarks track). Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. A third-party summary's 17 to 26 point gain from training is not verified against the paper and is not used.
about.what_it_tests: IFBench tests whether a language model follows written instructions that carry checkable constraints, such as counting, formatting, and word or character rules. It uses 58 new constraints that the models were not trained on, so it measures generalisation rather than memorised rules. Each reply is checked automatically by a rule-based function, and the paper reports that leading models of the time scored below 50 percent on the new constraints.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (14 November 2023) describes the instruction types.
about.what_it_tests: IFEval tests instruction following with about 500 prompts that carry verifiable instructions of 25 types, such as a word limit or a required format, so compliance can be checked by code. Publishers usually print prompt-level strict accuracy: the share of prompts where every instruction was followed.

about.maintainer: MathArena (ETH Zurich and INSAIT), using International Mathematical Olympiad problems
about.notes: 2025 is the MathArena paper year and the IMO sitting it describes. The official IMO homepage names the contest but does not print the exam format or a founding year.
about.what_it_tests: In the MathArena setup, the International Mathematical Olympiad is a proof contest of 6 problems. The model must write a full proof rather than a final answer. Expert graders write a scheme meant to resemble the contest scheme, including points for partial progress, and two judges score each anonymized solution. Each model produces four proofs per problem, and the reported score is the average of those runs.

about.notes: The arXiv paper "Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning" (3 November 2025) describes the three IMO-Bench parts; the proof and grading parts are separate benchmarks.
about.what_it_tests: IMO-AnswerBench is the short-answer part of IMO-Bench: 400 Olympiad-level problems whose answers can be checked automatically. The score is the share of problems answered correctly.

about.maintainer: OpenAI (internal evaluation, per the printed label)
about.notes: The name was not printed on the GPT-6 Astra system card section that discusses difficult ExploitGym problems.
about.what_it_tests: Impossible ExploitGym is printed on the GPT-6 Astra system card. By its name alone it would be a variant of the public ExploitGym benchmark whose tasks cannot be solved as designed. No source found describes this variant, so its task set and scoring are unconfirmed.

about.maintainer: Angelika Romanou and co-authors; dataset hosted by Cohere Labs
about.notes: The full exam collection is larger than the four-option include-base-44 subset used for the standard evaluation.
about.what_it_tests: INCLUDE measures knowledge and reasoning in the languages where the questions were originally written, using local exams rather than English questions translated into those languages. The full collection has 197,243 multiple-choice pairs from 1,926 examinations in 44 written languages, collected from local sources in 52 countries, covering academic exams, professional certifications and licenses, and regional licenses such as driving and marine licenses. The released base set keeps only four-option questions; the dataset card counts 22,637 of them. The paper reports accuracy.

about.maintainer: Minesh Mathew and co-authors (IIIT Hyderabad, IISER Pune, and CVC, Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona)
about.notes: The DocVQA dataset page returned no dataset text, so the counts and the scoring rule are taken from the paper, which points to docvqa.org.
about.what_it_tests: InfographicVQA asks questions about infographic images, which mix writing, graphics, layout, and charts. The paper reports 30,035 questions on 5,485 images, including items that need counting, sorting, or arithmetic, and answers that are a text span or a number. A prediction is scored with Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity, which still gives partial credit for a small string edit, and also with exact-match accuracy. The similarity gives no credit once the normalized edit distance reaches 0.5.

about.notes: Named on the Muse Spark Open model card. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: IntPhys 2 tests intuitive physics in video: the model watches short clips and has to tell physically possible events from impossible ones, across principles such as object permanence, immutability, spatio-temporal continuity and solidity. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: The old regulations file link no longer resolves, so the six-problem, 600-point account was not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: IOI tasks are the problems of the International Olympiad in Informatics, the secondary-school programming olympiad: six algorithmic problems over two contest days, each scored on partial subtasks up to 100 points, so a contest totals 600. Model cards print the total points on a stated year (IOI 2025).

about.maintainer: Paper authors Yuetai Li, Xiang Yue, Radha Poovendran and others
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (affiliations not shown on the abstract page); Alibaba attribution not confirmed. The paper was submitted May 25, 2026. Its author list shows no Alibaba affiliation on the page read, so the aggregator's Alibaba label is unconfirmed; this may be a different benchmark from any Alibaba-printed one. The paper reports the best of 36 models at 45.9 percent (Claude Opus 4.7 under Claude Code). The BenchLM figure of 33.4 for Qwen3.8-27B was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: JobBench tests AI agents on professional work that experts say they would want to hand off to an agent, rather than on tasks chosen for their economic value. It has 130 tasks across 35 occupations, and each task is a workspace of mixed and sometimes conflicting reference files that the agent must sort through. Outputs are graded against chains of rubrics that average about 35.6 binary criteria per task.

about.maintainer: Scaling Intelligence Lab at Stanford University
about.notes: The paper and repository do not define a nine-question Hard subset scored by TFLOPs against peak hardware.
about.what_it_tests: KernelBench asks a language model to replace a PyTorch machine-learning workload with a GPU kernel, in CUDA or another kernel language, that is both correct and fast. The paper uses 250 PyTorch workloads, and the repository splits the core set into 100 single operators, 100 fused patterns, and 50 full architectures. A kernel is correct when its outputs match the PyTorch reference on randomized inputs. The score, fast_p, is the share of kernels that are correct and faster than that PyTorch baseline by more than a chosen threshold p, using wall-clock time.

about.notes: The release page is the only description of this evaluation; OpenAI has not published its tasks or grading. A public repository named KernelGenBench is an unrelated operator-to-kernel benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: KernelGen 1P is an internal OpenAI evaluation of writing and optimizing compute kernels, part of the suite of real AI research tasks (debugging, kernel and training-recipe optimization, running experiments, improving another model) that OpenAI uses to measure how much a model speeds up its own research.

about.notes: Described only in the footnotes of the Kimi K2.7 Code model card; no public release of the tasks is named there.
about.what_it_tests: Kimi Claw 24/7 Bench is an in-house Moonshot AI benchmark for long-horizon agentic work in persistent, multi-day coworking tasks. It spans 17 professional scenarios with 610 evaluation points, in domains such as software engineering, ML research, recruiting, trading and marketing; every task runs through the OpenClaw harness. The score is the average pass rate over all evaluation points, averaged over 3 runs.

about.notes: The only public description is the footnote on the Kimi K3 model card (July 2026): the harness per model, the 80-task count and the refusal or fallback counts. The task contents, the scoring rule and the version history are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI.
about.what_it_tests: Kimi Code Bench is an in-house agentic coding benchmark of Moonshot AI, run inside a coding agent harness. Version 2.0 has 80 tasks, and the set includes cybersecurity and safety-related tasks, so the publisher also discloses how many tasks a model refused or handled with a fallback. The card prints one number per model and does not name the metric.

about.notes: The only public description is the Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (23 October 2026). The task contents and the grading are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI. The publisher says the Hard rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.
about.what_it_tests: Kimi Hallu Bench is an in-house factual-accuracy test of Moonshot AI. The prompts are challenging, de-identified requests drawn from practical work tasks, and fact-checking agents check every factual claim in the answer. The score is the claim-level hallucination rate, the share of claims that contain an error, so lower is better. A Hard split with tools is built from examples crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors.

about.notes: Mistral's 6 October 2026 post prints a 0 to 2 score with 2 labelled Exemplary, while the KORA models leaderboard prints a percentage.
about.what_it_tests: KORA measures how AI systems behave with children and teenagers. The project names 26 child-safety risks and evaluates models on synthetic conversations meant to resemble questions children ask, not on sessions with real children. Scenarios are grouped by age band: Big Kids (7 to 9), Tweens (10 to 12), and Teens (13 and older). The public models leaderboard prints one score as a percentage, and a higher score means the model responded more appropriately to the scenarios.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: first author Jon M. Laurent, with Samuel Rodriques and co-authors. arXiv 2407.10362, first submitted July 14, 2024. The successor LABBench2 (arXiv 2604.09554, FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, first submitted February 4, 2026) is a separate entry under the same family. The public release holds about 80% of the data, per the GitHub repository.
about.what_it_tests: LAB-Bench is a set of more than 2,400 multiple-choice questions that test practical biology research skills for language models and AI agents. The categories include recalling and reasoning over scientific literature, interpreting figures, using biology databases, and working with DNA and protein sequences. Models are scored on the share of questions they answer correctly and are compared with human expert biology researchers.

about.notes: The benchmarks.bio page describes 13 component benchmarks and a weighted average; aggregators describe 11 and an equal-weight mean, so these conflict. The v1.0 release date was not confirmed. Scores are not listed because aggregator figures disagree on the model set. The harness used to run the agent is reported separately and affects scores.
about.what_it_tests: LatchBio Capabilities is a composite score for how well AI agents analyse real biological data. Each component benchmark starts from a snapshot of real experimental data taken just before a key analysis step, and the agent must work out the biological result. A deterministic grader checks each answer, and the overall score is a weighted average of the pass rates.

about.notes: The vals.ai page (updated 12 October 2026) gives the scoring, the rubric sizes and the practice areas, but states neither a question count nor a launch date, and links a research paper without describing it, so the introduction year is left null. Do not conflate this with the VLAIR Legal Research study of October 2025 (Alexi, Counsel Stack, Midpage and ChatGPT), which appears only in search results and was not opened.
about.what_it_tests: Legal Research Bench tests whether an AI agent can answer realistic US legal research questions, using tools such as case-law search, web search and document retrieval to produce a supported answer. The tasks span eight practice areas: Administrative/Regulatory, Business & Commercial, Civil Litigation, Constitutional/Civil Rights, Criminal, Family, Health and Immigration. The questions, gold-standard answers and rubrics are written and peer-reviewed by practicing lawyers, and each question has 1 to 31 rubric items (mean 9.35). An LLM judge grades each response against the rubric; the primary metric is all-pass accuracy, where a question counts only if every rubric item is met, and the page also reports a partial-credit score by share of rubric points. Vals AI publishes the leaderboard.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with 173 scientists and Tacit Labs (a drug-development feedback startup) writing the tasks. The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 when read. The June 17, 2026 date and the task counts come from secondary coverage (AI Weekly, Let's Data Science, Gigazine), which agree. A reader comment says the questions are not public; not confirmed. Scores are omitted.
about.what_it_tests: LifeSciBench tests AI on the judgement work life-science researchers do, such as interpreting incomplete evidence, troubleshooting experiments and deciding what to do next. It has 750 expert-written tasks across seven workflows and seven biological domains. Each task includes supporting material and a grading rubric, and the answer is checked against that rubric (19,020 criteria in total).

about.notes: Lingo-Judge is a text classifier trained to agree with human raters, not a string-overlap metric such as BLEU.
about.what_it_tests: LingoQA is a visual question-answering benchmark for driving. The dataset has 28K short video scenarios and 419K free-text annotations, asking what is in the scene, what the vehicle should do next, why, and what deserves attention. The published evaluation suite has 1,000 examples. A learned text classifier, Lingo-Judge, reads the question, a human answer, and the model answer, without seeing the video, and the score is the share of answers it marks correct.

about.maintainer: Colin White, Samuel Dooley and co-authors (Abacus.AI, NYU and others)
about.notes: The 2024 paper defines this six-category benchmark; the livebench.ai homepage now shows a different LiveBench 2.0 long-horizon suite.
about.what_it_tests: LiveBench is a contamination-limited benchmark whose questions are drawn from recent math competitions, arXiv papers, news articles, and datasets. The paper version has 18 tasks in six categories: math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis, and every question has an objective ground-truth answer. Each question is scored from 0 to 1, each category score is the average of its tasks, and the LiveBench score is the average of the six category scores. Questions are added and replaced on a monthly schedule.

about.maintainer: LiveCodeBench authors (arXiv paper first author Naman Jain)
about.notes: The GitHub README (fetched, undated) lists release_v1 through release_v6, with release_v6 at 1,055 problems and an end date of April 2025, and describes pass@1 and pass@5. The arXiv abstract (submitted 12 March 2024, lead author Naman Jain) gives the 400-problem first release and the four scenarios, but it does not describe v6. The README names release_v6 rather than the label v6 printed on model cards, and no fetched page confirms that mapping, so cite the release by its date range and count.
about.what_it_tests: LiveCodeBench tests whether a code model can solve competitive programming problems it could not have seen in training. It collects new problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder and Codeforces contests, and each problem carries a release date, so models can be tested on problems released after their training cutoff. Beyond code generation, the benchmark covers self-repair, test output prediction and code execution. The release_v6 set holds 1,055 problems published between May 2023 and April 2025, and publishers print pass@1, scored by running generated code against test cases with a modified version of the APPS checker.

about.maintainer: LiveCodeBench Pro team (Zihan Zheng and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (13 June 2025) describes the problem sources and the pass@1 scoring; the Elo rating printed by Google model cards is the leaderboard's rating form and is not described in the abstract.
about.what_it_tests: LiveCodeBench Pro tests competitive programming with continuously updated problems from Codeforces, ICPC and the IOI, so the problems postdate the training data of the models. Olympiad medalists label the algorithmic category of every problem and review failed submissions. Publishers print either pass@1 on a difficulty tier or an Elo-style rating that places a model on the Codeforces scale.

about.maintainer: BIRD Team, HKU, and Google Cloud
about.notes: The site also publishes Base-Lite and Large-v1, which are different task sets from Base-Full v1.
about.what_it_tests: LiveSQLBench is a contamination-free text-to-SQL benchmark that adds new databases and tasks over time. The Base-Full v1 release, dated 4 September 2025, has 600 tasks on 22 real databases, covering business-intelligence queries and database management statements, with a hierarchical knowledge base for each database. A SELECT answer is checked by comparing its execution result with the gold SQL, and a management statement is checked with test cases. The score is the success rate, the share of tasks that pass those checks.

about.notes: Known only from the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL card label; the reading of the name is not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: LMArena v3 proxy is printed on the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model card among the conversational results; the card does not describe it. By its name it is an offline stand-in for LMArena human preference, scored by an automatic judge.

about.notes: The listed GitHub address is only the GitHub homepage, so it is not a source.
about.what_it_tests: LOCA-Bench tests an agent whose environment description runs to hundreds of thousands of tokens: the agent has to find and use the relevant parts of a long environment specification while acting in ReAct mode. The score is the task pass rate at the stated description length.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (with Zhipu AI); LongBench v2 authors include Yushi Bai and Shangqing Tu. Family dates from the original LongBench (arXiv 2308.14508, 2023, ACL 2024). LongBench v2 (arXiv 2412.15204) is from December 2024. The human baseline is 53.7% per the paper. Model scores are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: LongBench v2 tests whether language models can reason over very long inputs, with contexts from about 8,000 to 2 million words. It has 503 multiple-choice questions in six categories: single-document and multi-document question answering, long in-context learning, long dialogue history, code repository understanding and long structured data. Human experts scored about 54% under a 15-minute limit, which is the reference point for model scores.

about.notes: The paper scores this with F1 at a preferred length, not with a hallucination rate.
about.what_it_tests: LongFact is a prompt set for measuring factuality in long open-ended answers. GPT-4 generated the prompts across 38 topics, split into LongFact-Concepts and LongFact-Objects, with 30 prompts per topic and 1,140 prompts in each task. The SAFE method splits a response into individual facts and checks each fact by sending queries to Google Search and deciding whether the results support it. The aggregate score is an F1 that balances the percentage of supported facts with how many facts the response gives relative to a preferred length.

about.notes: This name appears only as a row on a model release page, with no public problem set or rubric.
about.what_it_tests: Longform Writing is the long-form writing evaluation Moonshot AI prints on its Kimi K2 release pages: the model writes extended pieces to a brief and the output is scored for quality, printed as a 0-100 score. The pages do not publish the prompts, the rubric or the judge.

about.maintainer: Haoning Wu, Dongxu Li, Bei Chen, and Junnan Li
about.notes: The project page marks it as a NeurIPS 2024 datasets and benchmarks release, and the pages opened here do not name a university.
about.what_it_tests: LongVideoBench tests understanding of long videos that come with subtitles. It has 3,763 web videos, grouped from a few seconds up to an hour, and 6,678 human-written multiple-choice questions in 17 categories. Each question first points at one or more moments, called the referred context, and then asks what is there or how those moments relate. The reported result is accuracy.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: first author Weihan Wang. The paper is arXiv 2406.08035 (June 2024), published at ICCV 2025. The video and question counts come from a third-party alphaXiv summary and were not checked against the paper's full text. Model scores are not given.
about.what_it_tests: LVBench tests whether vision-language models can understand very long videos, where the key facts can be spread across more than an hour of footage. It contains about 100 videos averaging over an hour, with roughly 1,500 question-answer pairs across six temporal comprehension tasks. Models are scored on accuracy against human performance.

about.notes: The card is the maintainer own document. Section 5.1.2.
about.what_it_tests: 112 tasks in a sandbox with GUI and CLI computer-use tools across surveillance, harmful content and scaled abuse; refusal rate without mitigations.

about.maintainer: Center for AI Safety and Scale AI (authors of the MASK paper); the Rectified variant is printed by xAI
about.notes: The page's revision line is dated 05 Jan 2026 and still describes only MASK.
about.what_it_tests: MASK tests whether a model lies when pressured to contradict what it believes, which is separate from whether it is accurate. For each of 1,500 examples (1,000 public, 500 held out) the model gets a pressure prompt, and its belief is then elicited by asking the same proposition neutrally three times; an LLM judge maps each answer to a resolution. A lie is counted when the statement made under pressure differs from the elicited belief, and the honesty score averages one minus the lie probability, so higher is more honest. The Rectified variant printed on the xAI card is not described in the paper.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (5 March 2021) describes the problems. MATH-500 is a fixed 500-problem subset and is a separate family.
about.what_it_tests: MATH tests competition mathematics with 12,500 problems from high-school competitions, each with a step-by-step solution. The score is the share of problems with the correct final answer.

about.notes: The paper "Let's Verify Step by Step" (31 May 2023) uses a representative subset of the MATH test set; the 500-problem split is published in the PRM800K repository.
about.what_it_tests: MATH-500 is a 500-problem subset of the MATH competition-math test set, released with OpenAI's PRM800K work so that models can be compared on one fixed slice. The score is the share of problems whose final answer is correct.

about.maintainer: SRI Lab at ETH Zurich and INSAIT
about.notes: The MathArena Apex page gives the maintainers, the launch date, the twelve problems, their sources, the selection rule and the scoring. Because the set grows, a value printed months apart may rest on a different problem count; the card does not say which revision it used.
about.what_it_tests: MathArena Apex is a small set of final-answer competition mathematics problems that frontier models could not solve when it was built. The launch set (18 August 2025) has 12 problems filtered from nearly 100 competitions, mostly from 2025: six from final-answer competitions and six converted from proof-based ones such as the IMO and team selection tests. A candidate problem was dropped if any of four frontier-model attempts answered it. The score is final-answer accuracy averaged over problems and repeated attempts, and the maintainers add problems over time.

about.maintainer: Renrui Zhang and co-authors (CUHK MMLab, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and UCLA)
about.notes: The six versions run from text-heavy to vision-only, so a single accuracy number can hide whether the model read the figure.
about.what_it_tests: MathVerse tests whether a multimodal model actually uses the diagram in a visual math problem. It collects 2,612 multi-subject problems with diagrams, and people rewrite each problem into six versions that move information between the text and the figure, giving 15K test samples. The project page reports accuracy on the testmini subset. The authors also score a written solution by extracting reasoning steps and marking each step, rather than only marking the final answer true or false.

about.maintainer: Ke Wang (lead author) and co-authors of the MATH-Vision work; project page at mathllm.github.io/mathvision
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 22 February 2024, lead author Ke Wang) gives the 3,040 problems, the competition source, the 16 disciplines and the 5 difficulty levels. The abstract does not describe scoring; the project page reports accuracy per subject and overall but does not explain the answer format or the answer-matching method.
about.what_it_tests: MathVision tests whether a multimodal model can solve competition mathematics problems that come with visual contexts. The set holds 3,040 problems sourced from real math competitions, spread across 16 mathematical disciplines and graded into 5 difficulty levels. The project page reports accuracy as a percentage, overall and per subject, on the full 3,040-example test set.

about.maintainer: Pan Lu and co-authors (UCLA, University of Washington, and Microsoft Research)
about.notes: The arXiv submission date is 3 October 2023, and the project page lists the conference version as ICLR 2024.
about.what_it_tests: MathVista tests mathematical reasoning that depends on a picture, including figures, charts, geometry diagrams, function plots, tables, scientific figures, and natural images. The full set has 6,141 examples, drawn from 28 existing multimodal datasets plus three new ones, IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA. Most reported results use testmini, a 1,000-example subset; the remaining 5,141 examples are the held-out test set. The published result is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Yile Liu and co-authors (Waseda University and OPPO AI Center)
about.notes: The prompts are parallel translations, not texts written separately in each language. A Qwen card says it reports accuracy on English plus the multilingual prompts, 23 settings in all.
about.what_it_tests: MaXIFE tests whether a model follows verifiable instructions in 23 languages. Each example joins one of 795 basic questions with one to three instructions, 1,667 instructions in a language, and the non-English text is a checked translation of the English set, giving 18,285 examples in all. Instructions about format, repetition, keywords, length, and similar constraints are scored by a program, either pass-or-fail or on a tiered point scale. Instructions about style, tone, or switching language are scored by a judge model.

about.notes: The paper does not define an MBPP+ variant.
about.what_it_tests: MBPP, Mostly Basic Programming Problems, asks a model to write a short Python program from a natural language description. The dataset has 974 crowd-sourced tasks meant to be solvable by entry-level programmers. Each task includes test cases, and the prompts consistently contain three input-output examples written as assert statements. A task counts as solved when the synthesized program passes those tests, and the paper reports the share of problems solved.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (v1 submitted 31 January 2026, lead author Chaithanya Bandi, 23 authors, v3 revised 19 May 2026) gives the server, tool and task counts and the 82.2% top pass rate at a 0.75 claim threshold. The Scale leaderboard page (updated 8 April 2026) gives the judge, the 75% pass rule and the pass-rate metric, and says Scale re-scored all models in April 2026 with a new judge, retry handling and a 100-call tool budget in place of the earlier 20-turn limit. So the paper's headline figure and older model-card numbers may come from different eval versions; the leaderboard page is the one to cite for current scores.
about.what_it_tests: MCP Atlas tests whether a language model can use real Model Context Protocol servers to answer multi-step questions. The prompts do not name the servers, tools or parameters, so the model has to find the right tools itself, call them correctly, recover from errors and synthesize a final answer; the paper describes 36 real MCP servers and 220 tools, and tasks span several servers. The benchmark has 1,000 human-authored tasks, and Scale publishes a 500-task public split while holding the other 500 back to protect leaderboard integrity. Each ground-truth answer is split into factual claims, an LLM judge (a Google model at temperature 0.0) scores each claim as 1, 0.5 or 0, and a task passes at 75% claim coverage. The metric that ranks models is the pass rate.

about.maintainer: eval-sys (GitHub project eval-sys/mcpmark); paper authors led by Zijian Wu
about.notes: The GitHub README of eval-sys/mcpmark describes MCPMark Verified as the default task set and says earlier task versions are deprecated and not directly comparable, so new results should be reported as MCPMark Verified. The arXiv paper 2509.24002 (2025, first author Zijian Wu) introduces the benchmark; the README was read undated, so its task count and any score it prints may change with the repository, and the paper version was not checked against it.
about.what_it_tests: MCPMark tests whether a model or agent can use real MCP servers to complete realistic tasks in working environments, rather than answer questions about them. The full suite covers Notion, GitHub, Filesystem, Postgres and Playwright, and the README gives 127 tasks; a smaller easy suite with 10 tasks per server is meant for smoke tests and CI. Each task ships with an automated verify.py script, and results are reported as pass@1, pass@k, pass^k and avg@k. MCPMark Verified is the current default task set, with every environment version-pinned and every verifier stabilised.

about.notes: A footnote says two models are left out because they refuse most of the questions, which still does not define the questions.
about.what_it_tests: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra launch page lists an internal evaluation named MedChemBench (Internal) in its science and health chart, printing a score for each model. The page does not describe the tasks, the inputs or the scoring, so what the test asks a model to do is not confirmed. The name points to medicinal chemistry, but no OpenAI text found says so.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (30 January 2025) describes the two subsets. Model cards usually print the MM subset separately, as "MedXpertQA MM".
about.what_it_tests: MedXpertQA tests expert-level medical knowledge and reasoning with 4,460 exam-style questions across 17 specialties and 11 body systems. It has a text subset and a multimodal (MM) subset whose questions come with medical images and rich clinical information. Scores are the share of questions answered correctly.

about.notes: Introduced in the GPT-6.1 Sol addendum. The October GPT-6 update reports the same name under a task-clipped metric, stored under separate benchmark ids. The paper PDF was not checked in full.
about.what_it_tests: MentalHealthBench scores model responses in mental-health conversations. The GPT-6.1 Sol addendum reports the mean percentage with standard error for overall, non-acute, high-acuity and emergent cases at maximum reasoning effort.

about.notes: Defined in the Muse Wonder model card (October 2026); the task set is not public. Not the same as other benchmarks named MemoryBench.
about.what_it_tests: MemoryBench is an internal Meta benchmark of recall across long multi-turn conversations of 64K to 100K tokens: the target facts are spread over several turns, with distractor conversations and injected turns that conflict with or later update them. An LLM judge scores each answer against weighted, question-specific rubric criteria.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (6 October 2022) describes the translation.
about.what_it_tests: MGSM tests multilingual math reasoning with 250 GSM8K word problems translated by hand into ten languages. The score is the share of problems with the correct final answer, averaged over languages.

about.notes: Cited in Claude Sonnet 5.5 System Card section 8.16 as arXiv:2411.02538. Paper not read.
about.what_it_tests: Culturally grounded knowledge comprehension across 11 languages: ten Indic languages and English.

about.notes: Known only from the MiMo-V2.6 card label.
about.what_it_tests: MiMo Code Bench is an in-house coding-agent benchmark that Xiaomi prints on its MiMo-V2.6 model card under Code Agent; the card does not describe its tasks, harness or metric.

about.notes: Known only from the MiMo-V2.6 card label.
about.what_it_tests: MiMo Cyber Bench is an in-house cybersecurity benchmark that Xiaomi prints on its MiMo-V2.6 model card; the card does not describe its tasks or metric.

about.notes: Known only from the MiMo-V2.6 card label.
about.what_it_tests: MiMo VisualCoding is an in-house benchmark that Xiaomi prints on its MiMo-V2.6 model card under Visual Agent, for coding tasks that start from or produce visual material; the card does not describe its tasks or metric.

about.maintainer: Kunhao Zheng, Jesse Michael Han, and Stanislas Polu (repository published under openai)
about.notes: The GitHub v1 freeze of August 2021 uses 244 test statements and 244 validation statements for Lean and Metamath.
about.what_it_tests: MiniF2F is a formal mathematics benchmark for neural theorem proving. It has 488 problem statements drawn from AIME, AMC, the International Mathematical Olympiad, and high-school and undergraduate courses, written for Metamath, Lean, and partially for Isabelle and HOL Light. The model must produce a proof that the proof assistant accepts. The paper reports the pass rate on a held-out test split, including Pass@1 and Pass@8.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (9 October 2024, Jun Shern Chan and co-authors) describes the 75 competitions and the medal rule. Publishers may run a subset (MLE-bench Lite) or a different time budget; a model card that prints "MLE-Bench" without further note does not say which.
about.what_it_tests: MLE-bench tests whether an AI agent can do machine learning engineering end to end. Its tasks are 75 Kaggle competitions: the agent must prepare the data, train models, run experiments and submit predictions. Each submission is placed against the human leaderboard of that competition, and the headline score is the share of competitions in which the agent reaches at least a bronze medal.

about.maintainer: MLS-Bench authors (28 authors on arXiv 2605.08678); project page at mls-bench.com
about.notes: The Lite subset is confirmed by the project page, which calls it the 'official 30-task Lite subset' on its leaderboard. The arXiv abstract (2605.08678, first submitted 2026-05-09, v3 2026-07-06) does not mention Lite. The project page names no organisation; it links a GitHub repository and a Hugging Face dataset and shows ten affiliated institutions, so the maintainer is given as the paper's authors. The page gives the scoring as the paper's normalized task metric without its formula. Aggregator scores are not used.
about.what_it_tests: MLS-Bench asks whether an AI system can invent generalizable ML methods rather than only tune existing ones. The full benchmark has 140 tasks across 12 domains, and each task asks an agent to propose one modular improvement to a targeted component, such as a loss, an attention variant, a sampler or a routing rule, then shows the change holds across models, datasets and seeds. MLS-Bench-Lite is the official 30-task subset shown on the leaderboard, and results are compared with a human reference labelled Human SOTA.

about.maintainer: Junjie Zhou and co-authors (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence and others)
about.notes: Model cards usually print M-Avg, the multiple-choice average, not the generation average.
about.what_it_tests: MLVU, Multi-task Long Video Understanding, asks a model questions about long videos whose lengths run from 3 minutes to more than 2 hours, including movies, surveillance, egocentric video, cartoons, and games. The paper defines 9 tasks, among them topic reasoning, anomaly recognition, summarization, and needle question answering, and it counts 1,730 videos and 3,102 questions. Multiple-choice tasks are scored by accuracy. Open-ended generation is scored by a judge model, and the paper averages the two groups separately as M-Avg and G-Avg.

about.notes: MiniMax states this only on the M2.7 launch post; there is no separate paper, and the name covers both an end-to-end accuracy and a skill-compliance rate.
about.what_it_tests: MM Claw is an evaluation set MiniMax built from tasks people commonly give OpenClaw agents. It covers work and life jobs, including personal learning plans, office document processing and delivery, scheduled research and investment advice, and code development and maintenance. The end-to-end score on that set is accuracy. MiniMax also reports a skill-compliance rate on the same name for 40 complex skills, each longer than 2,000 tokens.

about.maintainer: S Sakshi, Utkarsh Tyagi, Sonal Kumar, Ashish Seth, Ramaneswaran Selvakumar, Oriol Nieto, Ramani Duraiswami, Sreyan Ghosh, and Dinesh Manocha (University of Maryland, College Park, and Adobe)
about.notes: The homepage and the paper both describe the same 10k-clip question set; the homepage is where the answer options are visible.
about.what_it_tests: MMAU, Massive Multi-Task Audio Understanding and Reasoning, tests whether a model can answer questions about audio. It has 10k curated clips of speech, environmental sound, and music, paired with human-written questions and answers that require information extraction or reasoning across 27 skills. The project page shows the questions with listed answer options. The paper scores accuracy.

about.maintainer: Yuan Liu and co-authors (Shanghai AI Laboratory); the repository is run by the OpenCompass community
about.notes: The revised paper calls this release MMBench v1.1, and the live repository count does not match the 3,217 figure in the paper text.
about.what_it_tests: MMBench tests broad multimodal skill with single-answer multiple-choice questions in English and Chinese. The paper describes 3,217 questions across 20 ability dimensions, while the current repository lists 1,164 development questions and 1,784 test questions in each language. A free-form reply is mapped to a choice, by a matching rule when that works and otherwise by a language model. Under CircularEval the choices are rotated, the question is asked once for each order, and it counts as correct only when every pass is correct.

about.maintainer: Yubo Ma and co-authors (Nanyang Technological University and others)
about.notes: The project page still prints an older count, 1,091 questions on 135 documents averaging 47.5 pages; the November 2024 paper abstract is the later count.
about.what_it_tests: MMLongBench-Doc tests question answering over long PDF documents that mix text, images, charts, tables, and layout. The current paper counts 1,062 expert-written questions on 130 documents, with an average of 49.4 pages and 20,971 text tokens. About a third of the questions need evidence from more than one page, and 22.8% are written so the document does not contain the answer. The reported score is an F1 score over these answers, including the unanswerable ones.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (7 September 2020) describes the subjects.
about.what_it_tests: MMLU tests knowledge across 57 subjects, from elementary mathematics to law, with multiple-choice questions. The score is accuracy, usually with a stated number of few-shot examples.

about.maintainer: TIGER-Lab (University of Waterloo, Yubo Wang and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (3 June 2024) describes the construction and the ten-choice format.
about.what_it_tests: MMLU-Pro tests language understanding and reasoning across many academic and professional subjects. It takes the earlier MMLU, removes trivial or noisy questions, adds harder reasoning-focused ones and widens the answer choices from four to ten, so guessing helps less. The score is accuracy over the question set.

about.maintainer: Weihao Xuan and co-authors (University of Tokyo and others)
about.notes: The lite set is a shorter sample of the same parallel questions, not a different task.
about.what_it_tests: MMLU-ProX takes the reasoning-focused MMLU-Pro questions and presents the same items in 29 languages. Each language has 11,829 questions in the full set and 658 in the lite set, and each question is multiple choice with 10 options across 57 subjects. Translations were made by language models and then checked by expert review for accurate expression, terminology, and cultural relevance. The paper reports accuracy, including an average across the 29 languages.

about.maintainer: University of Edinburgh (Aryo Pradipta Gema and co-authors)
about.notes: The arXiv paper "Are We Done with MMLU?" (6 June 2024) describes the re-annotation.
about.what_it_tests: MMLU-Redux is a re-annotated subset of MMLU: 5,700 questions across all 57 subjects, checked by hand because about six percent of the original questions were found to be wrong. The score is accuracy.

about.notes: Released by OpenAI with the o1 models in September 2024 on Hugging Face. Publishers print one average over the languages; which languages and which prompting are used is not always stated.
about.what_it_tests: MMMLU (Multilingual MMLU) is the MMLU test set translated by professional human translators into 14 languages, including Arabic, Bengali, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Swahili and Yoruba. It tests the same multiple-choice knowledge questions across 57 subjects in those languages, so it measures knowledge and reasoning in languages other than English.

about.maintainer: MMMU team (Xiang Yue and co-authors; Ohio State University, Carnegie Mellon University and partners)
about.notes: The arXiv paper (November 2023) describes the question set; the validation split is the one model publishers usually report. MMMU-Pro (family mmmu-pro) is a harder 2024 revision with filtered questions and vision-only variants and is kept as its own family.
about.what_it_tests: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding) tests college-level reasoning over images and text together. It holds 11,500 questions drawn from exams, quizzes and textbooks across six disciplines (art and design, business, science, health and medicine, humanities and social science, technology and engineering) with 30 image types such as charts, diagrams, chemical structures and sheet music. Accuracy on the questions is the score.

about.maintainer: Xiang Yue (lead author) and co-authors of the MMMU team; code under the MMMU-Benchmark GitHub organization
about.notes: The arXiv paper (first submitted 4 September 2024, lead author Xiang Yue, latest revision 22 May 2025) gives the three construction steps, the option count and the vision-only setting. Its counts do not line up: it gives 1,730 questions in one place and 3,460 question-form items (1,730 standard plus 1,730 vision-only) in another, so cite the count with care. The GitHub README gives no question count or scoring method; the averaging rule comes from the paper's section 3.1.
about.what_it_tests: MMMU-Pro tests whether a multimodal model still understands multi-discipline questions once the shortcuts of the original MMMU are removed. The benchmark was built in three steps: questions that text-only models could answer were filtered out, the candidate options were increased from four to ten, and a vision-only setting embeds the whole question inside an image. The paper reports 1,730 questions, and the overall score is the average of the ten-option standard setting and the vision-only setting, with model answers read from an 'Answer: $LETTER' line.

about.maintainer: Lin Chen and co-authors (University of Science and Technology of China, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory)
about.notes: The project page says MMStar was accepted at NeurIPS 2024.
about.what_it_tests: MMStar tests multimodal understanding on items that were kept only when the image is needed. Humans selected 1,500 samples, with 250 for each of six capabilities and 18 finer axes. The six capabilities are coarse perception, fine-grained perception, instance reasoning, logical reasoning, science and technology, and mathematics. The main result is accuracy, and the paper also defines Multi-modal Gain and Multi-modal Leakage for separate analyses.

about.maintainer: Yilun Zhao (lead author) and co-authors; code and data under the yale-nlp GitHub organization
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 21 January 2025, lead author Yilun Zhao, 19 authors) gives the 3,000 questions, the 27 subjects and the four disciplines. The README gives the 1,529 videos and the question types but no accuracy formula, and it does not state the number of annotators; the GPT-4o judging is described for the released validation results, not as a fixed part of the benchmark definition.
about.what_it_tests: MMVU tests whether a model can reason about expert-level video in four core disciplines (Science, Healthcare, Humanities and Social Sciences, and Engineering) spanning 27 subjects. The set holds 3,000 expert-annotated questions over 1,529 specialized-domain videos. Each example comes with expert-annotated reasoning rationales and domain knowledge, and each question is either open-ended or multiple-choice. The README reports accuracy; its released validation results were judged with GPT-4o, and the repository's acc_evaluation.py script produces the scores.

about.notes: The only public description is the Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (23 October 2026). The task contents and the grading are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI.
about.what_it_tests: DECK-Arena is an in-house presentation-generation test of Moonshot AI on real-world queries. Models build slides through python-pptx, pptxjs and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with search and image generation. An automated grader calibrated on more than 10,000 human judgments compares the decks, and the result is an Elo score.

about.notes: The only public description is the Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (23 October 2026). The task contents and the grading are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI.
about.what_it_tests: Design Bench is an in-house graphic-design test of Moonshot AI, prompted directly and with reference-image few-shot examples. Models work through python-pptx, pptxjs and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with search and image generation. An automated grader calibrated on more than 10,000 human judgments compares the outputs, and the result is an Elo score.

about.notes: The only public description is the Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (23 October 2026). The task contents and the grading are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI. The page does not state the scoring scale.
about.what_it_tests: Three in-house finance tests of Moonshot AI. Financial Modeling grades formula linkage, financial logic and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. Financial Research grades whether a model produces auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. Business Operation tests long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment.

about.notes: The only public description is the Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (23 October 2026). The task contents and the grading are not public, so values cannot be reproduced outside Moonshot AI.
about.what_it_tests: xdev-bench-hard is an in-house set of expert-curated vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks built on source code. Most tasks reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore and Exim; the agent must exploit the target in a separate sandbox and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. Moonshot AI reports the share of problems solved at pass@3 and the average success rate, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

about.maintainer: Wenyi Hong and co-authors (Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI)
about.notes: The project page labels those six groups MR, LM, CM, MO, AO, and RC, and it reports separate dev and test averages.
about.what_it_tests: MotionBench tests fine-grained motion understanding in video. It has 8,052 manually written multiple-choice questions on clips from the web, public datasets, and synthetic scenes. The six question groups are motion recognition, location-related motion, camera motion, motion-related objects, action order, and repetition count. The reported result is accuracy.

about.maintainer: Kiran Vodrahalli and co-authors of the Michelangelo paper
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (listed by one wiki as Google DeepMind); the public MRCR dataset is attributed to OpenAI. The Michelangelo paper (arXiv 2409.12640, September 2024) defines MRCR as one of three tasks. The OpenAI release of the dataset was not confirmed on a primary source. The 8-needle and 256K-1M details come from benchmark listings, not the paper. Scores are omitted because listings disagree.
about.what_it_tests: MRCR (Multi-Round Coreference Resolution) tests whether a model can find one specific earlier item in a very long chat. The conversation contains many similar requests, such as poems or essays on overlapping topics, and the model must reproduce the output that matches the one the user asked for. The 8-needle variant hides eight such matching items, and results are reported at long context lengths such as 256K, 512K and 1M tokens.

about.notes: The grammar book and word list are released encrypted, with the password printed in the repository, so the test text stays off ordinary web crawls.
about.what_it_tests: MTOB (Machine Translation from One Book) asks a model to translate between English and Kalamang, a language with fewer than 200 speakers and almost no text on the web. The material is one grammar book, a bilingual word list, and a small set of parallel sentences. After examples used in the book are removed, 500 sentences are split into 400 for training and 100 for test. The paper scores each direction with chrF.

about.notes: The project site returned no text; the correspondence address on the paper is at bytedance.com.
about.what_it_tests: Multi-SWE-bench tests whether a model can edit a repository so that a reported software issue is fixed. It covers Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C, and C++, with 1,632 instances chosen by 68 expert annotators from 2,456 candidates. The task is to produce a patch that addresses the given issue. The primary score is the resolved rate, the percentage of issues resolved.

about.notes: The paper's author line names Scale AI, and the score is accuracy on the binary rubric.
about.what_it_tests: MultiChallenge tests whether a model can answer the last turn of a conversation while respecting what was said earlier. Each example is a conversation of at most 10 turns that ends with a user request, and the released set has 273 conversations. The four challenge types are instruction retention, inference memory of user information, reliable versioned editing, and self-coherence. A judge answers a yes-or-no rubric written for that example, and a yes means the response passed; the reported result is accuracy.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (14 April 2025) describes the languages and the parity measures; the abstract does not fix one scoring metric, so a printed value is stored with the metric label the publisher used.
about.what_it_tests: MultiLoKo tests multilingual knowledge with 500 locally relevant questions in each of 31 languages, plus translated versions that show how much an answer depends on the language of the question. Publishers print the average score across languages.

about.notes: The paper reports a pass rate from hidden unit tests in each language, not one named average across languages.
about.what_it_tests: MultiPL-E translates unit-test code generation benchmarks from Python into other programming languages. It translates HumanEval and MBPP, including the function signature, the comment, and simple unit tests, into 18 additional languages so the same problems can be scored in each language. A completion is judged correct only if it passes every unit test. Because generation is stochastic, the paper samples several completions per problem and reports an estimated pass rate.

about.notes: The paper dates the benchmark to a November 2023 submission and a CVPR 2024 version.
about.what_it_tests: MVBench tests temporal understanding of video. It has 20 tasks that cannot be solved from a single frame, made by turning static image tasks into dynamic ones, such as action sequence, moving direction, and counterfactual inference. Public video annotations are converted into multiple-choice questions, 200 per task, so the correct option is the annotated ground truth. The score is accuracy, and the paper also reports the average accuracy across tasks.

about.notes: The launch page is the only public mention found, and a name plus a percentage is not a definition of the task.
about.what_it_tests: An internal OpenAI evaluation named after the small NanoGPT language model training setup, listed with the self-improvement evaluations on the GPT-5.6 release page. The page prints only the name and a percentage per model; what the agent must do with the training run is not stated.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (first author Jingzhe Ding; 49 authors on arXiv; affiliations not shown on the abstract page); Alibaba attribution not confirmed. arXiv 2512.12730 was posted in December 2025 and accepted to ICML 2026 (PMLR 306). The abstract reports that even the strongest agents average below 40 percent test pass rate. The Alibaba label was not supported by the affiliations read.
about.what_it_tests: NL2Repo-Bench tests whether a coding agent can build a whole software project from a single natural-language requirements document. The agent starts with an empty workspace and must produce an installable Python library, across 104 tasks in nine library categories graded as easy, medium and hard. Scoring is execution-based, measuring the average share of each project's tests that pass.

about.maintainer: Not stated on the model cards
about.notes: The name suggests 63 languages, but the card never says that.
about.what_it_tests: NOVA-63 appears on the Qwen3.5 model cards in the Multilingualism block as one accuracy per model; by its name it covers 63 languages. The card gives no note on its content or source.

about.maintainer: Holger Caesar, Varun Bankiti, Alex H. Lang, Sourabh Vora, Venice Erin Liong, Qiang Xu, Anush Krishnan, Yu Pan, Giancarlo Baldan, and Oscar Beijbom
about.notes: The project site returned no text, so this follows the 2019 dataset paper (CVPR 2020 camera ready) rather than a model-card grounding score.
about.what_it_tests: nuScenes is a driving dataset for detecting and tracking objects around a vehicle. It has 1,000 scenes, each 20 seconds long, from 6 cameras, 5 radars, and 1 lidar, all with a full 360 degree field of view. Every scene is annotated with 3D bounding boxes for 23 classes and 8 attributes. The paper defines its own 3D detection and tracking metrics for those boxes, but it does not print the metric formulas in the abstract.

about.notes: Named on the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL card, which ran it on the official implementation or an internal scaffolding. Written as remembered; not re-read for this entry.
about.what_it_tests: OCR-Reasoning tests reasoning over text-rich images such as documents, charts, receipts and screenshots: the answer needs both reading the text and reasoning about it (calculation, logic, spatial and multidisciplinary knowledge). The score is accuracy.

about.notes: The same repository later added OCRBench v2, a separate set of 10,000 human-checked pairs, so a bare OCRBench name can mean either set.
about.what_it_tests: OCRBench tests whether a multimodal model can read text in an image and answer from it. The scored set has 1,000 manually checked question-answer pairs in five parts: text recognition, scene-text visual question answering, document-oriented visual question answering, key information extraction, and handwritten mathematical expression recognition. Those pairs come out of a wider study that uses 29 text datasets. The published result is a final score that adds the five part scores.

about.maintainer: Liunian Harold Li and co-authors (GLIP; code at microsoft/GLIP)
about.notes: ODinW-13 is this 13-dataset set; the paper is a CVPR 2022 submission first posted in 2021.
about.what_it_tests: ODinW, Object Detection in the Wild, is the transfer setting in the GLIP paper. It uses 13 public object-detection datasets from Roboflow, each asking the model to localize a different set of objects, including drone views, aquarium scenes, ego-centric hands, and thermal images. The paper reports average precision on this collection. The same table includes a zero-shot column and several few-shot columns.

about.notes: The two names stay apart because neither page states that one is the base version of the other.
about.what_it_tests: OfficeQA is printed on the GPT-5.4 release page among the professional evaluations with a pass rate per model and no further description. Databricks publishes OfficeQA Pro, an enterprise benchmark of grounded question answering over a corpus of U.S. Treasury Bulletins (parsing, retrieval and analysis across text and tables), and OfficeQA without the suffix is read as its base version.

about.notes: The arXiv abstract page (titled 'OfficeQA Pro: An Enterprise Benchmark for End-to-End Grounded Reasoning', v1 submitted 9 March 2026, lead author Krista Opsahl-Ong) gives the 133 questions, the corpus and the accuracy results for three frontier agents. Databricks is named as the maintainer from the Databricks tooling the page cites, not from an affiliation line that was read. A Databricks V2 (90 questions, about 120,000 pages) and a 48.12% figure appear only in search results and secondary write-ups, so they are not stated here; cite the 133-question v1 version.
about.what_it_tests: OfficeQA Pro tests whether an AI agent can answer questions that need grounded, multi-document reasoning over an enterprise document corpus. The corpus is the U.S. Treasury Bulletins, about 89,000 pages spanning nearly 100 years and more than 26 million numerical values, so the agent has to parse documents, retrieve the right pages and calculate across prose and tables. The benchmark has 133 questions, written by a team led by Krista Opsahl-Ong. The printed metric is accuracy, as a percentage. The paper reports that frontier agents scored under 5% from parametric knowledge alone, under 12% with web access, and averaged 34.1% when given the document corpus.

about.notes: The paper prints the second language as CPP, and a problem passes only when every organizer test case passes.
about.what_it_tests: OJBench tests competition-level programming. It has 232 problems from China's National Olympiad in Informatics and the International Collegiate Programming Contest, together with the test cases released by the organizers. A model may answer in Python or CPP. A solution is correct only if it passes every test case, and the reported metric is Pass@n, which counts a problem as passed when at least one of n solutions is correct.

about.maintainer: Linke Ouyang (lead author) and co-authors; code and dataset under the opendatalab GitHub organization (OpenDataLab)
about.notes: The arXiv abstract (submitted 10 December 2024, lead author Linke Ouyang, version 2 dated 25 March 2025, accepted at CVPR 2025) gives the nine sources, the layout categories and the attribute labels. The README's 1,651-page count does not say which version it belongs to, and its v1.6 entry adds 296 pages; the Overall formula is listed under the v1.5 change, so quote the version together with any score.
about.what_it_tests: OmniDocBench tests whether a model can parse PDF pages into structured content across varied document types, including handwritten notes and densely typeset newspapers. The paper describes nine document sources annotated with 19 layout categories and 15 attribute labels. The README gives 1,651 PDF pages across 10 document types, 5 layout types and 5 language types, and its metrics are normalized edit distance for text, TEDS for tables and CDM for formulas, combined in the leaderboard Overall score as ((1 - text Edit distance) * 100 + table TEDS + formula CDM) / 3.

about.maintainer: Paper authors from Humanlaya, BIGAI, xbench and M-A-P
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (per the arXiv affiliations); the aggregator's Alibaba label is not supported by the paper. The first version was submitted March 9, 2026 and the current version was revised October 8, 2026. Project code is at github.com/humanlaya/OneMillion-Bench. The expert-score leaderboard seen on a third-party site (dated 2026-08-03) was not verified and its model names were not captured.
about.what_it_tests: $OneMillion-Bench tests language agents on 400 expert-curated professional tasks in law, finance, industry, healthcare and natural science. The tasks ask agents to find authoritative sources, resolve conflicting evidence, apply domain rules and make constrained decisions, and each task carries a dollar value based on the time a senior professional would need. Responses are scored with an expert rubric covering factual accuracy, logical coherence, practical feasibility and professional compliance.

about.notes: Some figures are printed in the text only. The card states that lower is better for the flag rates; the direction of the others is taken from their own wording as a rate of unwanted behaviour.

Lower is better.

about.notes: Internal OpenAI evaluations described by the GPT-6.1 Sol addendum.

about.notes: The GPT-5 system card (arXiv 2601.03267) describes the design: 16 rollouts per challenge with pass@12 over the best set of rollouts. A release page that prints one number per model may use a different attempt budget or a different challenge mix; the suite is internal and changes between cards.
about.what_it_tests: OpenAI's internal capture-the-flag suite, used under its Preparedness Framework, asks a model to solve more than 100 publicly available CTF challenges across web, reverse engineering, binary and network exploitation, cryptography and miscellaneous categories. Challenges are sorted by the skill level they need (high school, collegiate, professional); collegiate and professional tasks require chaining two or more exploitation steps. The model works on a headless Linux machine with offensive tools, and the result is a pass rate over repeated attempts per challenge.

Models are compared without Trusted Access and with the Daybreak Blue or Daybreak Red access programmes. Higher values mean more tasks completed.

about.notes: Described only on the GPT-5 release page; implementation and grading details are referred to the system card.

The year 2026 is from the catalog's card date (2026-09-03) and the launch page's 2026 footer; the launch date itself is not stated in the text read. No scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: This OpenAI factuality evaluation measures the share of answers that contain at least one factual error, on de-identified ChatGPT conversations where users had flagged a factual error from an earlier model. The prompts are deliberately difficult and not representative of typical usage, so the result is not a general error rate. The test set is internal to OpenAI, and lower is better.

A run fails if the model does not acknowledge that search is unavailable, and the result is reported as a failure rate where lower is better. OpenAI's system card calls the test the Broken Search Tool evaluation.

about.notes: The family's exact name does not appear in the card. Which one the printed label means is not confirmed. No scores are given.

Each task has a safe route to completion; the score is the rate of unintended outcomes such as data disclosure or unauthorized transactions, overall and by type. Lower is better. Results are reported with and without the confirmation policy that tells the model when to pause for the user's approval.

The release page reports it as one percentage per model.

The taxonomies and grading are described in the October 2025 OpenAI post on strengthening ChatGPT responses in sensitive conversations; the prompt sets are internal.

Responses are graded against taxonomies of desired behaviour written with clinicians, and the score is the share of responses that comply.
